Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

The **Kennedy Center Honors** is an annual tribute recognizing [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts") contributions to [American culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States"). Presented annually since 1978, a December gala celebrates five honorees at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center") Opera House in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")[[1]](#cite_note-about-1) Chiefly awarded to individuals for lifetime achievements, honorees have occasionally included duos or musical groups, while collective honors have recognized one [musical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_theatre "Musical theatre"), one [television show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_show "Television show"), and one performing arts venue.[[2]](#cite_note-WaPo_2024-2)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[George Stevens Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Stevens_Jr. "George Stevens Jr.") created the Kennedy Center Honors with [Nick Vanoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Vanoff "Nick Vanoff") and produced the first gala in 1978. He was the producer and co-writer through the 2014 awards,[[3]](#cite_note-3) after which he sold the production rights to the Kennedy Center.

The idea for the Kennedy Center Honors began in 1977, after that year's 10th-anniversary White House reception and Kennedy Center program for the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") (AFI). [Roger L. Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_L._Stevens "Roger L. Stevens"), the founding chairman of the Kennedy Center, asked George Stevens Jr. (no relation), the founding director of the AFI, to hold an event for the center. Stevens Jr. asked Isaac Stern to become involved, and then pitched the idea to the television network [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS "CBS"), who bought it. With the first Honors event and honorees, CBS vice president for specials, Bernie Sofronski, stated:[[4]](#cite_note-wash_post-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5)

> George [Stevens] came to us with this. What turned us on is that this is the only show of its kind. In Europe and most countries, they have ways of honoring their actors and their athletes. England has its command performances for the queen. We see this as a national honoring of people who have contributed to society, not someone who happens to have a pop record hit at the moment ... Our intention is not to do just another award show. We're going to make an effort in terms of a real special.

The first host was [Leonard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Bernstein "Leonard Bernstein") in 1978, followed by [Eric Sevareid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Sevareid "Eric Sevareid") in 1979 (with [Gene Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Kelly "Gene Kelly") closing it) and [Beverly Sills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beverly_Sills "Beverly Sills") in 1980. [Walter Cronkite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Cronkite "Walter Cronkite") hosted from 1981 to 2002 and [Caroline Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Kennedy "Caroline Kennedy") hosted from 2003 to 2012. [Glenn Close](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Close "Glenn Close") hosted in 2013 and [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert "Stephen Colbert") hosted from 2014 to 2016.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Ricky Kirshner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Kirshner "Ricky Kirshner") and [Glenn Weiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Weiss "Glenn Weiss") of White Cherry Entertainment were the Executive Producers of the 38th annual Kennedy Center Honors (2015) after George Stevens Jr. stepped down.[[8]](#cite_note-8) There was no formal host in 2017, although Caroline Kennedy delivered an introduction. In 2018, mid-2021, and 2023 [Gloria Estefan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloria_Estefan "Gloria Estefan") hosted, [LL Cool J](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LL_Cool_J "LL Cool J") hosted in 2019, and [David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Letterman "David Letterman") hosted in late 2021. Queen Latifah hosted in 2024. There was no formal host in 2022, though several former honorees delivered an introduction. In 2022, David Jammy of Done+Dusted and Elizabeth Kelly of ROK Productions were hired to serve as Executive Producers.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

This awards show does not air live (with the exception of closed-circuit venues), but an edited version lasting approximately two hours is normally televised on CBS after Christmas. In 2024, the presentation added a half hour, making the show two and a half hours.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) Normally, the show has been aired between Christmas and New Year's on CBS television, but, in a departure from this tradition, the 2019 Kennedy Center Honors aired on regular television in early December and was later made available on CBS All Access. Due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the 2020 edition was postponed[[12]](#cite_note-12) and eventually held between May 17 and May 22, 2021, and the edited broadcast aired on June 6, 2021.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Since 2021, the annual Honors broadcast has been available to stream for a limited time through CBS platforms and Paramount+[[14]](#cite_note-14)

The 2025 Kennedy Center Honors ceremony, held at the Kennedy Center on December 7, 2025, was hosted by U.S. president [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"), thus marking the first time any sitting or former U.S. president hosted the Kennedy Center Honors.[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

### Selection process

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Selection process")]

Honoree recommendations are accepted from the general public,[[17]](#cite_note-17) and the Kennedy Center initiated a Special Honors Advisory Committee, which comprises members of the board of trustees as well as past honorees and distinguished artists.[[18]](#cite_note-18) The executive committee of the board of trustees selects the honoree recipients based on their impact and contributions to American culture and excellence in music, dance, theater, opera, motion pictures or television.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The selections are typically announced sometime between July and September. Most honorees are [Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans"), with non-U.S. citizen honorees typically hailing from elsewhere in the [anglosphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglosphere "Anglosphere").

## Events

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Kennedy_Center_Honors&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Events")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg/250px-Kennedy_Center_%2846399777861%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kennedy_Center_(46399777861).jpg)

The Kennedy Center lights up in rainbow colors every year in the weeks preceding the ceremony.

The invitation-only, weekend-long ceremony includes the Chairman's Luncheon, the State Department dinner, White House reception, and the Honors gala performances and supper.

The Chairman's Luncheon is held on Saturday at the [Kennedy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center "Kennedy Center"). Surrounded by the honorees, the chairman of the board of trustees launches the event with a welcoming speech. At that evening's reception and dinner at the [State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State"), presided over by the [Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State"), the honorees are introduced and the Honors medallions are presented by the chairman of the board.[[19]](#cite_note-kennedy-center.org-19) The wide rainbow-colored ribbon then hung around the necks of the recipients and prominently noticeable when the events are televised, symbolizes "a spectrum of many skills within the performing arts" according to creator [Ivan Chermayeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Chermayeff "Ivan Chermayeff").[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21)

On Sunday, there is an early-evening [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") reception,[[22]](#cite_note-22) traditionally hosted by the [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and the [First Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Lady_of_the_United_States "First Lady of the United States"), followed by the Honors gala performance at the Kennedy Center and supper.

Prior to 2017, there had been three occasions in which the president did not attend the gala performance. President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") did not attend in 1979 during the [Iran hostage crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran_hostage_crisis "Iran hostage crisis"); First Lady [Rosalynn Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalynn_Carter "Rosalynn Carter") served as his surrogate.[[23]](#cite_note-23) President [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") was on a trip to [Brussels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brussels "Brussels") and could not attend in 1989; First Lady [Barbara Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Bush "Barbara Bush") served as his surrogate.[[24]](#cite_note-24) President [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") was on a trip to [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest") and could not attend in 1994; First Lady [Hillary Rodham Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Rodham_Clinton "Hillary Rodham Clinton") served as his surrogate.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

For the 2015 gala performance, President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") joined First Lady [Michelle Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Obama "Michelle Obama") late after addressing the nation in a live telecast from the White House.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

In 2017, President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") and First Lady [Melania Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melania_Trump "Melania Trump") decided not to participate in events honoring recipients of the 2017 Kennedy Center Honor

Mercury

The planet Mercury has just under 400 craters. The wonderful part is that most of them are named for famous people in the arts: writers, artists and composers. The rule for inclusion is that “all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.”

*Haydn: Symphony No. 43 in E-Flat Major, Hob.I:43, “Mercury” – IV. Allegro (Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment; Frans Brüggen, cond.)*

In looking over the list, we find some 50 craters named after composers, conductors, and musicians. [Gluck](https://interlude.hk/skipping-town-christoph-willibald-gluck/) and [Debussy](https://interlude.hk/claude-achille-debussy/) rub shoulders with John Lennon and Machaut. They come from countries all over the world, from India to Italy, Austria to America, and China to Brazil. They are predominantly male, but [Alicia de Larrocha](https://interlude.hk/great-women-artists-shaped-music-v-alicia-de-larrocha/) (Spain) does sweep in as does Cai Wenji (China) and Umm Kulthum (Egypt).

*Strauss I: Merkurs Flugel, Walzer (Wings of Mercury, Waltz), Op. 83 (Slovak Sinfonietta, Žilina; Christian Pollack, cond.)*

*Holst: The Planets: III. Mercury, The Winged Messenger (Royal Scottish National Orchestra; David Lloyd-Jones, cond.)*

When you look at the map of Mercury recently developed by the US Geological Survey, we can find out where our composers are.

Sometimes the juxtapositions of names seem a bit random and other times, done with a clever sense of humour: Berlioz next to Carolan (top left), Purcell next to the painter van Dijck/Dyck (center top), and right in the middle of the planet is Mozart. Debussy is by Joplin (bottom left) and above Lennon, is Holst.

## Biography

Born in St. Petersburg, Russia, George Balanchine (1904–1983) is regarded as the foremost contemporary choreographer in the world of ballet. He came to the United States in late 1933 at the age of 29, accepting the invitation of the young American arts pa­tron Lincoln Kirstein (1907–96), whose great passions included the dream of creating a ballet company in America. At Balanchine’s behest, Kirstein was also prepared to support the formation of an American academy of ballet that would eventually rival the long-established schools of Europe.

This was the School of American Ballet, found­ed in 1934, the first product of the Balanchine–Kirstein collaboration. Several ballet companies directed by the two were created and dissolved in the years that followed, while Balanchine found other outlets for his choreography. Eventually, with a performance on October 11, 1948, the New York City Ballet was born. Balanchine served as its ballet master and principal choreographer from 1948 until his death in 1983.

Balanchine’s more than 400 dance works include *Serenade* (1934); *Concerto Barocco* (1941); *Le Palais de Cristal*, later renamed *Symphony in C* (1947); *Or­pheus* (1948); *The Nutcracker* (1954); *Agon* (1957); *Symphony in Three Movements* (1972); *Stravinsky Violin Concerto* (1972); *Vienna Waltzes* (1977); *Bal­lo della Regina* (1978); and *Mozartiana* (1981). His final ballet, a new version of Stravinsky’s *Variations for Orchestra*, was created in 1982.

He also choreographed for films, operas, revues and musicals. Among his best-known dances for the stage is *Slaughter on Tenth Avenue*, originally created for Broadway’s *On Your Toes* (1936). The musical was later made into a movie.

A major artistic figure of the 20th century, Bal­anchine revolutionized the look of classical ballet. Taking classicism as his base, he heightened, quick­ened, expanded, streamlined and even inverted the fundamentals of the 400-year-old language of aca­demic dance. This had an inestimable influence on the growth of dance in America. Although at first his style seemed particularly suited to the energy and speed of American dancers, especially those he trained, his ballets are now performed by all the ma­jor classical ballet companies throughout the world.

## 10 Things You Should Know

**1.** Affectionately known as “Mr. B.”  
 **2.** Was Artistic Director of New York City Ballet for 35 years. He co-founded New York City Ballet in 1948 with Lincoln Kirstein and served as the ballet master and principal choreographer until his death.  
 **3.** Made his on-stage debut when he was just ten. Balanchine appeared as the cupid in the Mariisnky Theatre Ballet Company production of *The Sleeping Beauty*.  
 **4.** Directed 10 ballets for Boston Ballet between 1963 and 1973. These included *Apollo* (1965), and *Scotch Symphony* (1965). Balanchine also served as Boston Ballet’s artistic advisor for several years.  
 **5.** Has a crater on Mercury named after him. Acquired by NASA on June 29, 2011, the crater radiates blue-colored rays that are similar in hue to the tutus in *Serenade*.  
 **6.** Created an estimated 465 works in his lifetime.  
 **7.** Recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Balanchine was one of five recipients to receive this award in 1983 from President Ronald Reagan, who praised Balanchine for “lifting our spirits and broadening our horizons through his talent and art.”  
 **8.** Credited with inventing the “neoclassical style.” He combined classical technique with explosive movements and energizing turns. His choreography was graceful yet full of speed and athletic prowess, stretching the boundaries of ballet.  
 **9.** Studied piano at the same conservatory as Tchaikovsky. As a pianist and the son of a well-known Georgian composer, Balanchine had a keen understanding of music theory and composition. He believed dance should showcase the music, rather than the other way around. He was often quoted as saying “See the music, hear the dance.”  
 **10.** Choreographed a ballet for 50 elephants. Balanchine was commissioned by the Ringling Bros., Barnum & Bailey Circus to create *Circus Polka* (1942), a ballet that featured 50 elephants and 50 ballerinas dancing to music by Igor Stravinsky.

## Timeline of George Balanchine’s Life

**1904:** Born in St. Petersburg, Russia.  
 **1913:** Begins studies at the Imperial Theater School.  
 **1920:** Choreographs his first piece, a duet entitled *La Nuit*. Enters the St. Petersburg Conservatory of Music.  
 **1925:** Joins Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes in Paris and becomes his principal choreographer. Balanchine also meets Igor Stravinsky, who will become a life-long friend and collaborator.  
 **1933:** Boston-born dance connoisseur Lincoln Kirstein persuades Balanchine to relocate to the United States.  
 **1934:** Kirstein and Balanchine establish the School of American Ballet. Soon after, they set up a touring company of dancers from the school and call it the American Ballet.  
 **1948:** Balanchine co-founds New York City Ballet (NYCB) with Kirstein. Balanchine will serve as NYCB’s ballet master and principal choreographer until his death.

**Ginger Rogers** (born **Virginia Katherine McMath**; July 16, 1911 – April 25, 1995) was an American actress, dancer, and singer during the [Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Hollywood_cinema "Classical Hollywood cinema") of Hollywood. She won an [Academy Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress "Academy Award for Best Actress") for her starring role in [*Kitty Foyle*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitty_Foyle_(film) "Kitty Foyle (film)") (1940), and performed during the 1930s in [RKO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RKO "RKO")'s [musical films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_film "Musical film") with [Fred Astaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Astaire "Fred Astaire"). Her career continued on stage, radio, and television throughout much of the 20th century.

Rogers was born in [Independence, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence,_Missouri "Independence, Missouri"), and raised in [Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"). She and her family moved to [Fort Worth, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Worth,_Texas "Fort Worth, Texas"), when she was nine years old. In 1925, she won a Charleston dance contest[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) that helped her launch a successful [vaudeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaudeville "Vaudeville") career. After that, she gained recognition as a [Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre "Broadway theatre") actress for her stage debut in *[Girl Crazy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girl_Crazy "Girl Crazy")*. This led to a contract with [Paramount Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Pictures "Paramount Pictures"), which ended after five films. Rogers had her first successful film roles as a supporting actress in *[42nd Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Street_(film) "42nd Street (film)")* (1933) and *[Gold Diggers of 1933](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Diggers_of_1933 "Gold Diggers of 1933")* (1933).

In the 1930s, Rogers's nine films with Fred Astaire are credited with revolutionizing the musical genre and gave [RKO Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RKO_Pictures "RKO Pictures") some of its biggest successes: *[The Gay Divorcee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gay_Divorcee "The Gay Divorcee")* (1934), *[Top Hat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Hat "Top Hat")* (1935) and *[Swing Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_Time_(film) "Swing Time (film)")* (1936). But after two commercial failures with Astaire, she turned her focus to dramatic and [comedy films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_film "Comedy film"). Her acting was well received by critics and audiences in films such as *[Stage Door](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_Door "Stage Door")* (1937), *[Vivacious Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivacious_Lady "Vivacious Lady")* (1938), *[Bachelor Mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_Mother "Bachelor Mother")* (1939), *[Primrose Path](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primrose_Path_(1940_film) "Primrose Path (1940 film)")* (1940), [*Kitty Foyle*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitty_Foyle_(film) "Kitty Foyle (film)") (1940), *[The Major and the Minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Major_and_the_Minor "The Major and the Minor")* (1942) and *[I'll Be Seeing You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I'll_Be_Seeing_You_(1944_film) "I'll Be Seeing You (1944 film)")* (1944). After winning the Oscar, Rogers became one of the biggest box-office draws and highest-paid actresses of the 1940s.[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1)

Rogers's popularity was peaking by the end of the decade. She reunited with Astaire in 1949 in the commercially successful *[The Barkleys of Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Barkleys_of_Broadway "The Barkleys of Broadway").* She starred in the successful comedy *[Monkey Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkey_Business_(1952_film) "Monkey Business (1952 film)")* (1952) and was critically lauded for her performance in *[Tight Spot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tight_Spot "Tight Spot")* (1955) before entering an unsuccessful period of filmmaking in the mid-1950s, and returned to Broadway in 1965, playing the lead role in *[Hello, Dolly!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hello,_Dolly!_(musical) "Hello, Dolly! (musical)")* More Broadway roles followed, along with her stage directorial debut in 1985 of an off-Broadway production of *[Babes in Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babes_in_Arms "Babes in Arms")*. She continued to act, making television appearances until 1987, and wrote an autobiography *Ginger: My Story* which was published in 1991. In 1992, Rogers was recognized at the [Kennedy Center Honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honors "Kennedy Center Honors"). She died of natural causes in 1995, at age 83.

During her long career, Rogers made 73 films. In 1999, she ranks number 14 on the [AFI's 100 Years...100 Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFI's_100_Years...100_Stars "AFI's 100 Years...100 Stars") list of female stars of classic American cinema.

**Fred Astaire** (born **Frederick Austerlitz**;[[1]](#cite_note-Billman-1) May 10, 1899 – June 22, 1987) was an American dancer, actor, singer, musician, choreographer, and presenter, whose career in stage, film, and television spanned 76 years. He is widely regarded as the "greatest popular-music dancer of all time".[[2]](#cite_note-2) His accolades include an [Honorary Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_Academy_Award "Honorary Academy Award"), as well as three [Golden Globe Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Awards "Golden Globe Awards"), three [Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Awards "Primetime Emmy Awards"), a [BAFTA Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award "BAFTA Award"), and a [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award").

As a dancer, he drew influences from many sources, including tap, classical dance, and the elevated style of [Vernon and Irene Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_and_Irene_Castle "Vernon and Irene Castle"). His trademark style greatly influenced the [American Smooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Smooth "American Smooth") style of [ballroom dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballroom_dance "Ballroom dance"). He called his eclectic approach "outlaw style", a following of an unpredictable and instinctive muse.

Astaire had a long dancing partnership with [Ginger Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginger_Rogers "Ginger Rogers"), with whom he co-starred in ten Hollywood musicals during the [classic age of Hollywood cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Hollywood_cinema "Classical Hollywood cinema"), including *[Top Hat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Top_Hat "Top Hat")* (1935), *[Swing Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_Time_(film) "Swing Time (film)")* (1936), and *[Shall We Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shall_We_Dance_(1937_film) "Shall We Dance (1937 film)")* (1937).[[3]](#cite_note-3) Astaire's fame grew in films like *[Holiday Inn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holiday_Inn_(film) "Holiday Inn (film)")* (1942), *[Easter Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Parade_(film) "Easter Parade (film)")* (1948), *[The Band Wagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band_Wagon "The Band Wagon")* (1953), *[Funny Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funny_Face "Funny Face")* (1957), and *[Silk Stockings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Stockings_(1957_film) "Silk Stockings (1957 film)")* (1957). For his performance in [Irwin Allen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irwin_Allen "Irwin Allen") and [John Guillermin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Guillermin "John Guillermin")'s disaster film, *[The Towering Inferno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Towering_Inferno "The Towering Inferno")* (1974), Astaire received his only competitive Academy Award nomination for [Best Supporting Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor "Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor"), and he won the [Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actor – Motion Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Award_for_Best_Supporting_Actor_–_Motion_Picture "Golden Globe Award for Best Supporting Actor – Motion Picture") and the [BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Actor_in_a_Supporting_Role "BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Supporting Role").

Astaire received [several honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_awards_and_nominations_received_by_Fred_Astaire "List of awards and nominations received by Fred Astaire") including an [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") in 1950, the [Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Globe_Cecil_B._DeMille_Award "Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award") in 1960, the [Film Society of Lincoln Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_Society_of_Lincoln_Center "Film Society of Lincoln Center") tribute in 1973, the [Kennedy Center Honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honors "Kennedy Center Honors") in 1978, and [AFI Life Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFI_Life_Achievement_Award "AFI Life Achievement Award") in 1980. He was inducted into the [Hollywood Walk of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Walk_of_Fame "Hollywood Walk of Fame") in 1960, [American Theatre Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Theatre_Hall_of_Fame "American Theatre Hall of Fame") in 1972, and the [Television Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_Hall_of_Fame "Television Hall of Fame") in 1989. In 1999, the [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute") named Astaire the fifth-greatest male star of Classic Hollywood cinema in [100 Years... 100 Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFI's_100_Years...100_Stars "AFI's 100 Years...100 Stars").

**Eugene Curran Kelly** (August 23, 1912 – February 2, 1996) was an American dancer, actor, singer, director and choreographer. He was known for his energetic and athletic dancing style. Kelly sought to create a new form of American dance accessible to the general public, which he called "dance for the common man".[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) He starred in, choreographed, and, with [Stanley Donen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Donen "Stanley Donen"), co-directed some of the best-regarded [musical films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_film "Musical film") of the 1940s and 1950s.

Kelly is best known for his performances in *[An American in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_American_in_Paris_(film) "An American in Paris (film)")* (1951), which won the [Academy Award for Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture") and *[Singin' in the Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singin'_in_the_Rain "Singin' in the Rain")* (1952), which he and Donen directed and choreographed. He received a nomination for the [Academy Award for Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor "Academy Award for Best Actor") for his role as Joseph "Joe" Bradley" in *[Anchors Aweigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchors_Aweigh_(film) "Anchors Aweigh (film)")* (1945). Kelly's director debut was *[On the Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Town_(film) "On the Town (film)")* (1949), which he co-directed with Donen and also played the lead role. Later in the 1950s, as musicals waned in popularity, he starred in *[Brigadoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigadoon_(1954_film) "Brigadoon (1954 film)")* (1954) and *[It's Always Fair Weather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Always_Fair_Weather "It's Always Fair Weather")* (1955), the last film he directed with Donen. His solo directorial debut was *[Invitation to the Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invitation_to_the_Dance_(film) "Invitation to the Dance (film)")* (1956), one of the last MGM musicals, which was a commercial failure.

Kelly made his film debut in *[For Me and My Gal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For_Me_and_My_Gal_(film) "For Me and My Gal (film)")* (1942) with [Judy Garland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Garland "Judy Garland"), with whom he also appeared in *[The Pirate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pirate_(1948_film) "The Pirate (1948 film)")* (1948) and *[Summer Stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Stock "Summer Stock")* (1950). He also appeared in the [dramas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)") *[Black Hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hand_(1950_film) "Black Hand (1950 film)")* (1950) and *[Inherit the Wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inherit_the_Wind_(1960_film) "Inherit the Wind (1960 film)")* (1960),[[4]](#cite_note-DiLeo2002-4) for which he received critical praise.

He continued as a director in the 1960s, with his credits including *[A Guide for the Married Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Guide_for_the_Married_Man "A Guide for the Married Man")* (1967) and *[Hello, Dolly!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hello,_Dolly!_(film) "Hello, Dolly! (film)")* (1969),[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) which received an [Oscar nomination for Best Picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Picture "Academy Award for Best Picture").[[8]](#cite_note-Oscars1970-8)[[9]](#cite_note-NY_Times-9) He co-hosted and appeared in *[Ziegfeld Follies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ziegfeld_Follies_(film) "Ziegfeld Follies (film)")* (1946), *[That's Entertainment!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's_Entertainment! "That's Entertainment!")* (1974), *[That's Entertainment, Part II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's_Entertainment,_Part_II "That's Entertainment, Part II")* (1976), *[That's Dancing!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's_Dancing! "That's Dancing!")* (1985), and *[That's Entertainment, Part III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's_Entertainment,_Part_III "That's Entertainment, Part III")* (1994).

His innovations transformed the Hollywood musical, and he is credited with almost single-handedly making the ballet form commercially acceptable to film audiences.[[10]](#cite_note-Billman-10) According to dance and art historian Beth Genné, working with his co-director Donen in *Singin' in the Rain* and in films with director [Vincente Minnelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincente_Minnelli "Vincente Minnelli"), "Kelly ... fundamentally affected the way movies are made and the way we look at them. And he did it with a dancer's eye and from a dancer's perspective."[[2]](#cite_note-:0-2) Kelly received an [Academy Honorary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Honorary_Award "Academy Honorary Award") in 1952 for his career achievements; the same year, *An American in Paris* won six Academy Awards, including Best Picture. He later received lifetime achievement awards in the [Kennedy Center Honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Center_Honors "Kennedy Center Honors") (1982) and from the [Screen Actors Guild](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_Actors_Guild "Screen Actors Guild") and [American Film Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Film_Institute "American Film Institute"). In 1999, the American Film Institute also ranked him as the [15th greatest male screen legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AFI's_100_Years...100_Stars "AFI's 100 Years...100 Stars") of [Classic Hollywood Cinema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Hollywood_cinema "Classical Hollywood cinema").

**Charles Edward Anderson Berry** (October 18, 1926 – March 18, 2017) was an American guitarist, singer, and songwriter who was one of the pioneers of [rock and roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll "Rock and roll"). Nicknamed the "[Father of Rock and Roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorific_nicknames_in_popular_music "Honorific nicknames in popular music")", he refined and developed [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") into the major elements that made rock and roll distinctive with songs such as "[Maybellene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maybellene "Maybellene")" (1955), "[Roll Over Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roll_Over_Beethoven "Roll Over Beethoven")" (1956), "[Rock and Roll Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Music_(song) "Rock and Roll Music (song)")" (1957), and "[Johnny B. Goode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_B._Goode "Johnny B. Goode")" (1958).[[1]](#cite_note-1) Writing lyrics that focused on teenage life, [consumerism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumerism "Consumerism"), and music itself, and developing a music style that included guitar [solos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_solo "Guitar solo") and [showmanship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_showmanship "Guitar showmanship"), Berry was a major influence on subsequent [rock music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music").

Born into a middle-class family in [St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis "St. Louis"), Berry had an interest in music from an early age and gave his first public performance at [Sumner High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sumner_High_School_(St._Louis) "Sumner High School (St. Louis)"). While still a high school student, he was convicted of [armed robbery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_robbery "Armed robbery") and was sent to a [reformatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformatory "Reformatory"), where he was held from 1944 to 1947. After his release, Berry settled into married life and worked at an automobile assembly plant. By early 1953, influenced by the guitar [riffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riff "Riff") and showmanship techniques of the [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues") musician [T-Bone Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-Bone_Walker "T-Bone Walker"), Berry began performing with the [Johnnie Johnson Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnnie_Johnson_(musician) "Johnnie Johnson (musician)"). His break came when he traveled to Chicago in May 1955 and met [Muddy Waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muddy_Waters "Muddy Waters"), who suggested he contact [Leonard Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Chess "Leonard Chess"), of [Chess Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_Records "Chess Records"). With Chess, he recorded "Maybellene"—Berry's adaptation of the country song "[Ida Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ida_Red_(song) "Ida Red (song)")"—which sold over a million copies, reaching number one on *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_(magazine) "Billboard (magazine)")*'s rhythm and blues chart.

By the end of the 1950s, Berry was an established star, with several hit records and film appearances and a lucrative touring career. He had also established his own St. Louis nightclub, Berry's Club Bandstand.[[2]](#cite_note-2) He was sentenced to three years in prison in January 1962 for offenses under the [Mann Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mann_Act "Mann Act")—he had transported a 14-year-old girl across state lines for the purpose of having sex. After his release in 1963, Berry had several more successful songs, including "[No Particular Place to Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Particular_Place_to_Go "No Particular Place to Go")", "[You Never Can Tell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Never_Can_Tell_(song) "You Never Can Tell (song)")", "[Nadine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadine_(song) "Nadine (song)")" and the [novelty song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_song "Novelty song") "[My Ding-a-Ling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Ding-a-Ling "My Ding-a-Ling")"—his only number-one single. However, none of them achieved the same lasting impact of his 1950s songs, and by the 1970s he was more in demand as a nostalgia performer, playing his past material with local backup bands of variable quality.

Berry was among the first musicians to be inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") on its opening in 1986; he was credited with laying "the groundwork for not only a rock and roll sound but a rock and roll stance."[[3]](#cite_note-3) Berry is included in several of *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")* magazine's "greatest of all time" lists; he was ranked fifth on its 2004 and 2011 lists of the [100 Greatest Artists of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_100_Greatest_Artists_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Artists of All Time") and 2nd greatest guitarist of all time in 2023.[[4]](#cite_note-immortals-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame's [500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/500_Songs_That_Shaped_Rock_and_Roll "500 Songs That Shaped Rock and Roll") includes three of Berry's: "Johnny B. Goode", "Maybellene", and "Rock and Roll Music".[[6]](#cite_note-6) "Johnny B. Goode" is the only rock-and-roll song included on the [Voyager Golden Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyager_Golden_Record "Voyager Golden Record").
